FARMER PIET

By: Anina Peens | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On the foot of the Southern Drakensberg, a small farming community is in disbelief after one of their own played foul…

Unique Selling Point:
Tucked in the mountainous region of the Eastern Cape, a farming community in Barkly East is devastated by the actions of a member of their own community... An upright farmer stealing from pensioners.

Summary:
It’s one of the most basic investment models in agriculture; Piet has a farm where he can grow livestock. Koos lives in the city but wants to invest in livestock. It is a low risk-, no brainer investment. Koos gives Piet money to buy sheep. His return on investment? Offspring is shared between Piet and Koos. Koos can have his money back -including the return on investment-in just one season. Or, he can grow his share, not having to do anything. These investors usually ‘forget’ about the investment, and after a few years, their stock triple. Except if the host farmer has a hidden agenda…And it turns out, Piet Bekker from Aliwal North in the Eastern Cape had a few. He conned more than 30 investors including the towns’ pastor and doctor. Other investors were local pensioners investing their life savings, on Piet’s farm. Piet became a multimillionaire, and the investors are now scraping together the few cents they have left, to fight Piet to court, hoping they would get some of their money back. But according to Piet, he did nothing wrong and although he has recently been sequestrated, he is still convincing people to invest in livestock.


Further information:
Piet Bekker is a model citizen. Well known in his community for being an upright farmer...but not to be messed with, because he can shoot. He is also known as a wealthy commercial farmer, farming sheep and lucerne. He is trusted and people look up to the man who drives around town with his brand new two million Rand Toyota Land Cruiser (he bought this after his sequestration).

But it is starting to buzz in hushed tones, around Aliwal Noord…it may not be Piet’s own money that he’s flashing.
We have access to a group of 30 people who have all been scammed by Piet Bekker. They come from all walks of life, from doctors to pensioners; From Pretoria and Johannesburg to Bloemfontein, Somerset West and Cape town, they have lost millions of their life savings.
They didn’t know of each other at first and thought they were alone, fighting against Piet and his super connections in the police and his constant threats and bullying. But then, they learnt there were other victims too and formed a group to exchange notes. Not surprisingly, the modus operandi was identical and together, Piet owes them over 100 million Rand.

The same template of agreement is used for all the investors to sign to ‘join’ Bekker’s farming venture. It seems that he picked investors who live far away from the farm, to make it a logistical challenge to visit the farm. None of the investors have ever seen any of the livestock. None of them were ever given access when they asked to see their stock. There would always be an excuse, either it was due to drought, and Piet was too busy trying to feed animals or there were floods, and the farm was not accessible. Whenever the investors put pressure on him, Piet would pay small ‘insignificant’ amounts into their accounts to keep them quiet… Meanwhile, telling them to pray, as life on the farm is hard. He would often tell them that vast numbers of animals died in the drought or drowned in the flood.

The investors coined it a pyramid scheme disguised as a farming operation. Piet was selling the same fictional livestock to all his investors.

Excuses plied up. One victim kept track of WhatsApp communication between himself and Piet over a period of a year. The victim begs Piet to pay him, as he lost his job, but Piet have excuse after excuse.

Eventually, two of the investors filed for Piet’s sequestration in February this year.

LEGAL ACTION…BUT STILL NO PAYOUT

When the liquidators came to write up the stock, Piet was supposed to have over 10 thousand Dorper sheep on the farm, according to the contracts that he had signed with investors. But there was only one old dorper ewe around. Although 750 fat merino ewe, belonging to Piet, were roaming the farm. In all the contracts, Piet promised investors that he will mark their animals with white tags…there were no animals with white tags. And it is not clear how Piet planned to distinguish between the animals of the different investors, if they all had white tags.

A TWIST OF EVENTS
The animals on the farm all belonged to Piet’s company, Abbot Ann. It’s a closed corporation with two members: Piet and an African man, whose brother is the provincial police commissioner. When one investor opened a case of fraud against Piet at the Aliwal North police station, the police said, it’s a civil case, they cannot investigate.
To make matters worse, it seems that Piet is not to be held accountable.
Piet must’ve planned this scheme, paperwork now reveals. He cooked the books.
When investors made payments for livestock, Piet used the money to buy livestock from auctions. He had the auctioneer make out the invoice in his personal name. Then, as soon as the invoice was written, he told the auctioneering company, he had made a mistake, the animals must be bought into his CC. He thus has two receipts. He used this in his court case, arguing that he is not to be held accountable, because the company owned the stock. But all the stock was in his personal name.
It emerged in court, that all the stock of all the investors had died, or was stolen, or fell off cliffs… but Piet forgets that his own contracts with his investors hold him accountable to replace stock if they die or are stolen. But a contract seems to be just a piece of paper, for Piet.

WHAT NOW?

As legal cases are piling up against Piet, the investors fear that Piet may be a flight risk. He has often made it clear to the community that he has Swiss bank accounts and various offshore accounts. He said as much to the investors, telling them that he will sell all his assets and put the money in his offshore accounts for no one to reach. Lawyers now aim to file for an order to seize Piet’s passport.

Press Release:


Holy Sheep
He was a model citizen in the farming community of Barkly East in the Eastern Cape. A God-fearing commercial farmer with a loyal circle of friends. He was wealthy, too, by all accounts and promised similar riches for some of his closest friends and several others from a lucrative investment project. It was a simple blueprint: his investors would buy cattle and sheep and he would farm them on their behalf. Leaning on their shared religious devotion, his investment base grew impressively and his scheme blossomed into a multi-million rand operation. Then, as they so often do, things turned sour and what appeared a legitimate and profitable business imploded. The investors, the majority of whom are pensioners, lost everything. Carte Blanche investigates.

An upright farmer stealing from pensioners. Summary: It’s one of the most basic investment models in agriculture; Piet has a farm where he can grow livestock. Koos lives in the city but wants to invest in livestock. It is a low risk-, no brainer investment. Koos gives Piet money to buy sheep. His return on investment? Offspring is shared between Piet and Koos. Koos can have his money back -including the return on investment-in just one season. Or, he can grow his share, not having to do anything. These investors usually ‘forget’ about the investment, and after a few years, their stock triple. Except if the host farmer has a hidden agenda…And it turns out, Piet Bekker from Aliwal North in the Eastern Cape had a few. He conned more than 30 investors including the towns’ pastor and doctor. Other investors were local pensioners investing their life savings, on Piet’s farm. Piet became a multimillionaire, and the investors are now scraping together the few cents they have left, to fight Piet to court, hoping they would get some of their money back. But according to Piet, he did nothing wrong and although he has recently been sequestrated, he is still convincing people to invest in livestock. Further information: Piet Bekker is a model citizen. Well known in his community for being an upright farmer...but not to be messed with, because he can shoot. He is also known as a wealthy commercial farmer, farming sheep and lucerne. He is trusted and people look up to the man who drives around town with his brand new two million Rand Toyota Land Cruiser (he bought this after his sequestration). But it is starting to buzz in hushed tones, around Aliwal Noord…it may not be Piet’s own money that he’s flashing. We have access to a group of 30 people who have all been scammed by Piet Bekker. They come from all walks of life, from doctors to pensioners; From Pretoria and Johannesburg to Bloemfontein, Somerset West and Cape town, they have lost millions of their life savings. They didn’t know of each other at first and thought they were alone, fighting against Piet and his super connections in the police and his constant threats and bullying. But then, they learnt there were other victims too and formed a group to exchange notes. Not surprisingly, the modus operandi was identical and together, Piet owes them over 100 million Rand. The same template of agreement is used for all the investors to sign to ‘join’ Bekker’s farming venture. It seems that he picked investors who live far away from the farm, to make it a logistical challenge to visit the farm. None of the investors have ever seen any of the livestock. None of them were ever given access when they asked to see their stock. There would always be an excuse, either it was due to drought, and Piet was too busy trying to feed animals or there were floods, and the farm was not accessible. Whenever the investors put pressure on him, Piet would pay small ‘insignificant’ amounts into their accounts to keep them quiet… Meanwhile, telling them to pray, as life on the farm is hard. He would often tell them that vast numbers of animals died in the drought or drowned in the flood. The investors coined it a pyramid scheme disguised as a farming operation. Piet was selling the same fictional livestock to all his investors. Excuses plied up. One victim kept track of WhatsApp communication between himself and Piet over a period of a year. The victim begs Piet to pay him, as he lost his job, but Piet have excuse after excuse. Eventually, two of the investors filed for Piet’s sequestration in February this year. LEGAL ACTION…BUT STILL NO PAYOUT When the liquidators came to write up the stock, Piet was supposed to have over 10 thousand Dorper sheep on the farm, according to the contracts that he had signed with investors. But there was only one old dorper ewe around. Although 750 fat merino ewe, belonging to Piet, were roaming the farm. In all the contracts, Piet promised investors that he will mark their animals with white tags…there were no animals with white tags. And it is not clear how Piet planned to distinguish between the animals of the different investors, if they all had white tags. A TWIST OF EVENTS The animals on the farm all belonged to Piet’s company, Abbot Ann. It’s a closed corporation with two members: Piet and an African man, whose brother is the provincial police commissioner. When one investor opened a case of fraud against Piet at the Aliwal North police station, the police said, it’s a civil case, they cannot investigate. To make matters worse, it seems that Piet is not to be held accountable. Piet must’ve planned this scheme, paperwork now reveals. He cooked the books. When investors made payments for livestock, Piet used the money to buy livestock from auctions. He had the auctioneer make out the invoice in his personal name. Then, as soon as the invoice was written, he told the auctioneering company, he had made a mistake, the animals must be bought into his CC. He thus has two receipts. He used this in his court case, arguing that he is not to be held accountable, because the company owned the stock. But all the stock was in his personal name. It emerged in court, that all the stock of all the investors had died, or was stolen, or fell off cliffs… but Piet forgets that his own contracts with his investors hold him accountable to replace stock if they die or are stolen. But a contract seems to be just a piece of paper, for Piet. WHAT NOW? As legal cases are piling up against Piet, the investors fear that Piet may be a flight risk. He has often made it clear to the community that he has Swiss bank accounts and various offshore accounts. He said as much to the investors, telling them that he will sell all his assets and put the money in his offshore accounts for no one to reach. Lawyers now aim to file for an order to seize Piet’s passport. Extra Budget Items: 2 extra presenter days, 3 nights accommodation and fuel. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): On the foot of the Southern Drakensberg, a small farming community is in disbelief after one of their own played foul…
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Tucked in the mountainous region of the Eastern Cape, a farming community in Barkly East is devastated by the actions of a member of their own community... An upright farmer stealing from pensioners.
metadata.Summary: It’s one of the most basic investment models in agriculture; Piet has a farm where he can grow livestock. Koos lives in the city but wants to invest in livestock. It is a low risk-, no brainer investment. Koos gives Piet money to buy sheep. His return on investment? Offspring is shared between Piet and Koos. Koos can have his money back -including the return on investment-in just one season. Or, he can grow his share, not having to do anything. These investors usually ‘forget’ about the investment, and after a few years, their stock triple. Except if the host farmer has a hidden agenda…And it turns out, Piet Bekker from Aliwal North in the Eastern Cape had a few. He conned more than 30 investors including the towns’ pastor and doctor. Other investors were local pensioners investing their life savings, on Piet’s farm. Piet became a multimillionaire, and the investors are now scraping together the few cents they have left, to fight Piet to court, hoping they would get some of their money back. But according to Piet, he did nothing wrong and although he has recently been sequestrated, he is still convincing people to invest in livestock.
metadata.Further information: Piet Bekker is a model citizen. Well known in his community for being an upright farmer...but not to be messed with, because he can shoot. He is also known as a wealthy commercial farmer, farming sheep and lucerne. He is trusted and people look up to the man who drives around town with his brand new two million Rand Toyota Land Cruiser (he bought this after his sequestration). But it is starting to buzz in hushed tones, around Aliwal Noord…it may not be Piet’s own money that he’s flashing. We have access to a group of 30 people who have all been scammed by Piet Bekker. They come from all walks of life, from doctors to pensioners; From Pretoria and Johannesburg to Bloemfontein, Somerset West and Cape town, they have lost millions of their life savings. They didn’t know of each other at first and thought they were alone, fighting against Piet and his super connections in the police and his constant threats and bullying. But then, they learnt there were other victims too and formed a group to exchange notes. Not surprisingly, the modus operandi was identical and together, Piet owes them over 100 million Rand. The same template of agreement is used for all the investors to sign to ‘join’ Bekker’s farming venture. It seems that he picked investors who live far away from the farm, to make it a logistical challenge to visit the farm. None of the investors have ever seen any of the livestock. None of them were ever given access when they asked to see their stock. There would always be an excuse, either it was due to drought, and Piet was too busy trying to feed animals or there were floods, and the farm was not accessible. Whenever the investors put pressure on him, Piet would pay small ‘insignificant’ amounts into their accounts to keep them quiet… Meanwhile, telling them to pray, as life on the farm is hard. He would often tell them that vast numbers of animals died in the drought or drowned in the flood. The investors coined it a pyramid scheme disguised as a farming operation. Piet was selling the same fictional livestock to all his investors. Excuses plied up. One victim kept track of WhatsApp communication between himself and Piet over a period of a year. The victim begs Piet to pay him, as he lost his job, but Piet have excuse after excuse. Eventually, two of the investors filed for Piet’s sequestration in February this year. LEGAL ACTION…BUT STILL NO PAYOUT When the liquidators came to write up the stock, Piet was supposed to have over 10 thousand Dorper sheep on the farm, according to the contracts that he had signed with investors. But there was only one old dorper ewe around. Although 750 fat merino ewe, belonging to Piet, were roaming the farm. In all the contracts, Piet promised investors that he will mark their animals with white tags…there were no animals with white tags. And it is not clear how Piet planned to distinguish between the animals of the different investors, if they all had white tags. A TWIST OF EVENTS The animals on the farm all belonged to Piet’s company, Abbot Ann. It’s a closed corporation with two members: Piet and an African man, whose brother is the provincial police commissioner. When one investor opened a case of fraud against Piet at the Aliwal North police station, the police said, it’s a civil case, they cannot investigate. To make matters worse, it seems that Piet is not to be held accountable. Piet must’ve planned this scheme, paperwork now reveals. He cooked the books. When investors made payments for livestock, Piet used the money to buy livestock from auctions. He had the auctioneer make out the invoice in his personal name. Then, as soon as the invoice was written, he told the auctioneering company, he had made a mistake, the animals must be bought into his CC. He thus has two receipts. He used this in his court case, arguing that he is not to be held accountable, because the company owned the stock. But all the stock was in his personal name. It emerged in court, that all the stock of all the investors had died, or was stolen, or fell off cliffs… but Piet forgets that his own contracts with his investors hold him accountable to replace stock if they die or are stolen. But a contract seems to be just a piece of paper, for Piet. WHAT NOW? As legal cases are piling up against Piet, the investors fear that Piet may be a flight risk. He has often made it clear to the community that he has Swiss bank accounts and various offshore accounts. He said as much to the investors, telling them that he will sell all his assets and put the money in his offshore accounts for no one to reach. Lawyers now aim to file for an order to seize Piet’s passport.
